lessons.title: <stdfloat>: Fixed-Width Floating-Point Types
lessons.motivation: The types `float`, `double`, and `long double` have existed in C++ since its C heritage, but they carry a fundamental flaw: the standard never guaranteed their exact sizes in bytes. On most x86 platforms `float` is 32-bit IEEE 754 and `double` is 64-bit, but this is a de-facto norm rather than a language requirement. On certain embedded and DSP platforms the picture is different. For code that needs exact IEEE 754 semantics — network protocols, file formats, machine-learning libraries — this ambiguity causes portability problems. C++23 addresses this by introducing the `<stdfloat>` header with five new fixed-width floating-point types.
lessons.theory:
Before C++23, programmers who needed guaranteed precision wrote `typedef float float32_t;` — but that is merely an alias, not a new type. Two aliases for the same type cannot serve as the basis for function overloading, and the compiler cannot distinguish `float32_t` from `float`. C++23 solves this by introducing truly distinct types in the language's type system.

The `<stdfloat>` header defines up to five types: `std::float16_t` (IEEE 754 binary16, half precision), `std::float32_t` (IEEE 754 binary32, single precision — matches `float` on most platforms), `std::float64_t` (IEEE 754 binary64, double precision), `std::float128_t` (IEEE 754 binary128, quad precision — requires hardware support), and `std::bfloat16_t` (Brain Float 16, a format developed by Google/Intel). The standard only provides a type if the platform supports it; on x86-64 with GCC/Clang, all four except `float128_t` are typically available.

`bfloat16_t` deserves special attention. Unlike `float16_t`, which has 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits, `bfloat16_t` has the same 8 exponent bits as `float32_t` but only 7 mantissa bits. This means the same value range as `float32_t` at half the memory footprint. That is precisely why Google TPU, Intel AMX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch use bfloat16 for neural-network weights: training stability demands a wide dynamic range (to avoid overflow/underflow), not maximum mantissa precision.

In practice all new types support arithmetic operators and work with `std::numeric_limits<T>`. `std::format` and `std::print` format them correctly. Initializing from `float` literals requires an explicit cast (`static_cast`) — implicit narrowing in brace-initialization is forbidden. The key advantage over the old `typedef` approach is that these types are distinct in the type system, enabling overloaded functions that accept `float16_t` and `float32_t` as different arguments.

examples.title: Sizes and precision of the new types
examples.description: Checking the sizes of all available types from `<stdfloat>` and their precision via `std::numeric_limits`.
examples.expectedOutput:
sizeof float16_t:  2
sizeof float32_t:  4
sizeof float64_t:  8
sizeof bfloat16_t: 2
float32_t max digits10: 9
float64_t max digits10: 17
float16_t max digits10: 5

examples.title: bfloat16 for storing neural-network weights
examples.description: A practical ML scenario: storing weights in `bfloat16_t` instead of `float32_t` halves memory usage. Arithmetic is performed via explicit cast to `float`.

lessons.title: `std::byteswap`: Byte Swapping and Byte-Order Conversion
lessons.motivation: Before C++23, reversing the bytes of an integer required `__builtin_bswap32(x)` on GCC/Clang or `_byteswap_ulong(x)` on MSVC — non-standard extensions that broke portability. `std::byteswap`, `std::to_underlying` and `std::unreachable` were all standardised in C++23 in the same wave of proposals cleaning up low-level utilities. `to_underlying` and `unreachable` are covered in lesson m1-l5. This lesson focuses on `std::byteswap` — the only one of the three tied directly to numeric arithmetic: it accepts only integer types and returns the same type with its bytes reversed. The typical use case is converting between host byte order and network byte order when working with network protocols or binary file formats.
lessons.theory:
`std::byteswap` (header `<bit>`, P1272) is a portable `constexpr` function that reverses the bytes of any integer type. Before C++23 you had to use `__builtin_bswap32` / `__builtin_bswap64` on GCC/Clang or `_byteswap_ulong` / `_byteswap_uint64` on MSVC — none of those extensions were `constexpr`.

`std::byteswap` accepts any integral type — `uint8_t`, `uint16_t`, `uint32_t`, `uint64_t`, signed `int`, and so on — and returns the same type with its bytes reversed. The function is `constexpr`, so the swap can happen at compile time. For `uint8_t` (a single byte) the result equals the input — there is nothing to reverse.

Primary use cases:
- **Network byte order**: internet protocols (TCP, IP, DNS) use big-endian; most x86/x64 processors use little-endian. `byteswap` converts between them.
- **Binary file formats**: PNG, JPEG, PDF and many others store numbers in big-endian. Reading them on a little-endian system requires `byteswap` on each numeric field.
- **Hash algorithms**: several hash functions need byte reversal when processing input data.

The other two C++23 additions from the same «low-level utilities» group — `std::to_underlying` and `std::unreachable` — are covered in lesson m1-l5, where they fit naturally alongside enum semantics and exhaustive switch expressions.

examples.title: std::byteswap: byte-order conversion
examples.description: Converting between host byte order and network byte order. The function works in a `constexpr` context — a value can be converted at compile time.
examples.expectedOutput:
host:    0x12345678
network: 0x78563412
round-trip: 0x12345678
port 8080 in network order: 0x901f
PNG magic LE: 0x474e5089
examples.explanation: `std::byteswap(0x12345678)` reverses four bytes: 12→78, 34→56, 56→34, 78→12, giving `0x78563412`. A double swap recovers the original — this is true for any integer type. `constexpr` lets you convert a port number or magic constant at compile time with zero runtime overhead. The PNG magic `0x89504E47` reads as ASCII «‰PNG» in big-endian; on a little-endian machine it becomes `0x474E5089`.

examples.title: std::byteswap for all integer sizes
examples.explanation: For `uint8_t` (one byte) the swap is trivial: the value is unchanged. For `uint16_t` two bytes are exchanged: `AB CD` → `CD AB`. For `uint32_t` all four are reversed: `AB CD EF 12` → `12 EF CD AB`. For `uint64_t` all eight bytes are reversed. Signed types work too: `0x00000001` as int32 has bytes `00 00 00 01`, which after swapping becomes `01 00 00 00` = `0x01000000`.

lessons.title: `std::out_ptr` and `ranges::shift_left`/`shift_right`
lessons.motivation: Two practically useful C++23 additions close long-standing pain points. `std::out_ptr` eliminates the awkward two-step pattern of receiving a raw pointer from a C API and then wrapping it in a `unique_ptr` — the whole operation now fits in a single call with no leak window between the two steps. `std::ranges::shift_left` and `std::ranges::shift_right` provide a straightforward way to shift elements in a range in-place, replacing indirect workarounds with `std::rotate` or manual `std::move`.
lessons.theory:
`std::out_ptr` and `std::inout_ptr` (header `<memory>`, P1132) solve the problem of interoperating smart pointers with C APIs that take `T**` as an output parameter. The typical pattern before C++23: declare `T* raw = nullptr`, pass `&raw` to the C API, then manually call `.reset(raw)` or re-construct the `unique_ptr`. `std::out_ptr(ptr)` creates a temporary adaptor object that holds a `T*` and, when destroyed (at the end of the full expression), calls `ptr.reset(raw_ptr)` with whatever value the C API wrote. `std::inout_ptr` does the same but additionally extracts the current raw pointer from the smart pointer before passing it in — needed for C APIs that may reuse an already-allocated buffer. Both work with `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`, and any type that has a `.reset()` member.

`std::ranges::shift_left` and `std::ranges::shift_right` (header `<algorithm>`, P1243) move elements of a range n positions to the left or right in-place. `shift_left(r, n)` moves each element n positions toward the beginning: `r[i] = move(r[i+n])`. It returns a subrange of the valid elements (the first `size - n` elements). `shift_right(r, n)` symmetrically shifts toward the end and returns the last `size - n` elements. Elements "pushed off" the edge remain in the range in a valid but unspecified state — they are not destroyed, but their values must not be relied upon. The range's size does not change. If `n >= size`, an empty subrange is returned. Practical uses include ring-buffer implementations, sliding-window algorithms, and efficient removal of elements from the front without `erase(begin())`, which would move the entire contents.

examples.title: `ranges::shift_left` and `ranges::shift_right`: in-place shifting
examples.description: `shift_left` and `shift_right` shift range elements and return a subrange of valid elements.
examples.expectedOutput:
after shift_left(2), valid: 3 4 5 
vector size still: 5
after shift_right(1), valid: 1 2 3 4 
sliding window: 30 40 50 60 70
examples.explanation: `shift_left(data, 2)` moves elements: `data[0]←data[2]`, `data[1]←data[3]`, `data[2]←data[4]`. It returns a subrange of the first `size-n = 3` valid elements: `{3, 4, 5}`. `data[3]` and `data[4]` are left in a valid-but-unspecified state — the vector size does not change. In the sliding-window example, after `shift_left(buf, 2)` the first three positions hold `{30, 40, 50}`, and the two trailing positions are overwritten with `60` and `70`.

examples.title: `std::out_ptr`: smart pointers and C APIs
examples.description: `std::out_ptr` replaces the two-step pattern of "get a raw pointer from a C API, then manually call `.reset()`". The adaptor calls `.reset()` itself when it is destroyed at the end of the expression.
examples.expectedOutput:
old pattern value: 42
out_ptr pattern value: 99
both resources properly destroyed
